messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
Kwame is a 33-year-old African American man who came to treatment at his wife’s urging after months of telling himself he should be able to manage on his own. He works as a social media manager for a nonprofit, spending most of his days in an open-plan office monitoring feeds, drafting posts, and responding quickly when stories begin to trend. Before this, he had worked overseas as a relief worker in a war zone, a role he had taken on with a strong sense of purpose. What happened there is the point his life now divides around.

During one deployment, Kwame was traveling with a small team delivering supplies in an area where shelling had become more frequent. He remembers the trip in fragments rather than as a smooth sequence. What stands out are pieces: the vehicle slowing, a sudden explosive crack that seemed to tear the air apart, people shouting over one another, dust and debris forcing their way into his mouth and eyes, and the sense that danger could come again from any direction. In the confusion, he was trying to work out where to move, who was injured, what was happening around him, but what stays with him most is the feeling that there was no safe side to turn toward. Later, back in the U.S., he learned that the people responsible would likely never face any consequences. That fact lodged in him with a particular bitterness. He has come to say, with flat certainty, that what happened was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it.

In the weeks after returning home, Kwame noticed that he did not want to think about the incident directly. If an image or bodily feeling associated with it started to surface, he would pull away from it almost automatically, as if stepping back from the edge of something dangerous. He describes detaching himself from the memories, keeping them at a distance rather than letting himself stay with them. At first this felt like control. He threw himself into work, kept conversations factual, and avoided lingering on questions from his wife about what that period had been like. When she tried gently to ask what he remembered, he would say he was tired or change the subject. He was not trying to be cold; he felt that if he let himself think about it fully, he would lose his grip.

At the same time, everyday life began to feel organized around watching for threat. In public he constantly scanned his surroundings, checking doorways, windows, sudden movements, and the expressions of strangers. Even in ordinary settings—a grocery store, a parking garage, his own office—his attention moved restlessly across the environment. In the open office where he now works, he finds himself tracking footsteps behind him, noticing who enters the room, and orienting toward abrupt noises before he can stop himself. Slack notifications, chairs scraping, or someone dropping a metal water bottle can make him jolt hard enough that coworkers look over. He is embarrassed by how jumpy he seems, but he cannot settle. What frightens him is not only the startle itself but the feeling that his body reacts before he does, as if he cannot rely on himself to stay composed or think clearly when it matters.

That fear has begun to color how he sees himself. Kwame had once trusted his judgment under pressure, but now he is less certain. At work he rereads simple captions several times and loses track of what he was about to post. During meetings, he can hear colleagues talking and still realize he has not absorbed what was said. He worries that his concentration is slipping in ways other people will notice. When a campaign required rapid responses to graphic news coming out of another conflict zone, he found his attention scattering between the screen and the room around him, checking and rechecking both. He began volunteering to work from home more often, telling his supervisor it helped productivity. In reality, home felt easier to control. Even there, though, he remained on guard, listening for sounds in the hallway and checking the locks more than once before bed.

His marriage has narrowed around these habits. His wife has noticed how absent he can seem when the topic of his relief work comes up, as though he leaves the room without moving. She has also noticed how quickly he reacts to sudden noise and how difficult it is for him to stay present during dinner if the restaurant is crowded or unpredictable. Kwame feels guilty about this, but guilt sits beside resentment: resentment that the people responsible have faced no consequences, that the event can still enter his life while those who caused it remain untouched. He repeats that injustice to himself often, with the same stunned conviction each time.

He sought help only after a recent incident at work when a loud crash from a stack of equipment being knocked over made him lurch out of his chair and lose the thread of a client call he was leading. Afterward he sat staring at his screen, unable to concentrate, shaken by how little confidence he had in his own reactions. What brought him in was not one single memory but the accumulation of this daily watchfulness, the effort of not thinking, and the sense that his world has become organized around bracing. He says he wants to feel present with his wife again and to trust himself at work, but what he is most afraid of is that if he stops holding the memories at a distance, he will discover he has less control over himself than he already fears.
